title: Run a full lesson with zero technology
mechanism_check: Identify exactly what the tech was doing: delivering content, holding attention, or running the timer. Replace the function, not the device.
Check the clock: a no-tech lesson needs a visible time anchor or pacing drifts — a wall clock, a wristwatch, or a student timekeeper.
Scan the room: can every student see a board? If not, the lesson must be voice- and movement-based, not board-based.
improvised_tools: Chalkboard, whiteboard, or butcher paper taped to the wall
A student timekeeper with a wristwatch or the wall clock
Student 'scribes' who restate key points aloud so the room hears them twice
steps: Write the objective in one sentence on the board before anything else.
Teach the core idea in a 7-minute direct burst — short on purpose.
Run guided practice aloud: you model, the whole class responds in unison, individuals get cold-called.
Assign the independent task on paper with a visible finish line: 'five problems, then we compare.'
Close with three students restating the objective in their own words; correct drift immediately.
stop_conditions: Stop the lecture burst if several students are lost — you are going too fast, not them being inattentive; restart from a concrete example.
Stop and reset the room if noise kills comprehension; silence first, content second.
If time runs short, drop the extra practice problems, never the closure — a lesson without closure is just noise.

title: Improvise a writing surface from household materials
mechanism_check: Check what writing implement you actually have: marker, chalk, charcoal, grease pencil. The surface must match the implement — markers bead on glass, chalk needs a matte rough face.
Test in a corner first: does the mark erase or wipe without ghosting? A surface you cannot erase is a poster, not a board.
Check the sightline: the surface must face the seats, not the window — backlight kills readability.
improvised_tools: A smooth cabinet door or desktop plus dry-erase marker (wipes off melamine/painted surfaces)
Brown paper bags cut open and taped flat as a giant scratch sheet
A shower curtain liner as a reusable writing overlay with washable markers
steps: Choose the implement first, then the surface that erases with it.
Mount the surface at standing height, facing the class, away from window glare.
Test-erase a corner; if it ghosts, lay paper over it instead of fighting the surface.
Use fat lines and block letters — thin handwriting is unreadable past the second row.
When the period ends, wipe it clean so it is ready next time; never leave yesterday's lesson up.
stop_conditions: Stop if the marker does not erase from the surface — forcing it stains permanently; switch to paper.
Stop writing smaller to fit more — if the lesson does not fit the surface, cut the lesson, not the letter size.
Do not write on a borrowed surface you cannot clean (a neighbor's painted door, a rented wall); use taped paper instead.

title: Teach fractions with paper and scissors
mechanism_check: Confirm the real obstacle: students cannot picture 'three-fourths' as a quantity, not that they cannot memorize rules. The fix is a physical part they can hold.
Check that everyone has the same paper size; mismatched sheets make comparison lies out of true.
Verify scissors are safe and counted — lost scissors mid-lesson will eat the whole period.
improvised_tools: Plain paper cut into equal strips or circles — identical sizes are the whole trick
Scissors (shared safely, counted out and back in)
Crayons or pens to label pieces before cutting so parts stay matched to wholes
steps: Give every student identical paper strips; have them label the whole '1' before any cutting.
Fold and cut one strip into halves, another into fourths — label each piece as it is cut.
Ask: which is bigger, one-half or two-fourths? Let them lay pieces on top of each other to prove it.
Stack pieces to find equivalents: two fourths cover one half exactly.
End with the rule derived from the paper: the top number counts pieces, the bottom number names the size.
stop_conditions: Stop cutting new shapes if students cannot label the first set — more pieces without labels is just confetti.
Stop if the pieces become the toy instead of the model; collect scissors and finish the comparison verbally.
If the class is still stuck after the hands-on, drop to halves only and master those before fourths.

title: Demo pendulum motion with string, a ruler, and coins
mechanism_check: Identify the concept: period depends on length, not on weight or swing size. The demo must isolate length as the single variable.
Check the anchor point: a shaky hand holding the string ruins timing — the string needs a fixed pivot (taped to a desk edge, a door frame).
Confirm you have a counting method: ten swings timed on a wristwatch beats guessing at one.
improvised_tools: String or shoelace plus a coin or washer as the bob
A ruler to measure and change the string length precisely
A wristwatch or wall clock to time ten swings
steps: Tape the string to a fixed pivot; hang the coin so it swings freely without hitting anything.
Pull it aside a small, consistent angle and release; count ten full swings and record the time.
Shorten the string by half and repeat the ten-swing timing with the same coin.
Swap the coin for a heavier object at the same length and time again — the time barely changes.
State the mechanism aloud: length sets the speed of the swing; weight and push size barely matter.
stop_conditions: Stop if the string stretches or the pivot slips — fix the anchor before trusting any number.
Stop adding variables; if students suggest changing two things at once, hold to one variable per test.
If the room cannot stay quiet enough to count, switch to visual comparison (two pendulums side by side) instead of timing.

title: Improvise a chemistry demo with kitchen supplies
mechanism_check: Pick ONE reaction concept per demo: acid-base, gas production, or density layering. Kitchen demos that try to show everything show nothing.
Check safety before spectacle: no open flame with unknown fumes, no sealed containers with gas-producing mixes, no tasting anything.
Verify quantities are small: a tablespoon-scale demo is controllable; a cup-scale demo is a cleanup event.
improvised_tools: Baking soda plus vinegar for controlled gas production
Red cabbage boiled in water as a pH indicator (pink in acid, green-blue in base)
Oil, water, and food coloring in a clear bottle for density layers
steps: State the prediction question first: 'What will you see when I pour this?' — prediction is the whole point.
Add the reagent slowly in front of the class; narrate what you observe, not what you wish they saw.
For the indicator: drop vinegar into cabbage water (pink), then add baking-soda solution drop by drop until it swings green.
Connect observation to mechanism in one sentence per demo; never lecture over the fizz.
Dispose down the sink with water; wipe the demo area before the next class enters.
stop_conditions: Stop immediately if a mixture foams out of its container — the scale was too big; redo smaller next time, not bigger.
Never mix bleach with vinegar or any acid — chlorine gas is the hard line; this demo family stays at food-grade reagents only.
If a student has asthma or chemical sensitivity, run the demo at arm's length from the room's far side or skip it; no demo is worth a medical incident.

title: Build a biology observation station from jars and yard finds
mechanism_check: Check what the station is for: observation skills (draw, describe, measure), not keeping pets. Specimens are tools, not mascots.
Survey the yard or lot for what is actually available: leaves, insects, soil, rocks — build the station around the finds, not a wish list.
Confirm the light situation: living specimens need daylight placement; the station lives by a window, not in a dark corner.
improvised_tools: Glass jars with perforated lids as observation chambers
Magnifying glasses, or a phone camera zoom as the backup lens
Student observation logs: date, drawing, one measurement, one question
steps: Assign a collection mission with strict limits: two specimens per student, nothing alive longer than a school day unless its habitat comes with it.
Set up each jar with a label: name, found-where, found-when.
Run the observation routine: 5 minutes silent looking, then draw exactly what you see (no cartoons), then measure one thing.
Each student writes one question their specimen raises; post the questions as the station's research board.
Release or return living specimens the same day; log what was learned, not what was owned.
stop_conditions: Stop the station if specimens become a distraction economy (trading, naming contests) — the jars close until observation resumes.
Never collect stinging insects, unknown fungi, or anything a student is allergic to; when in doubt, photograph it instead of catching it.
If a specimen dies in the jar, that is the lesson: log why, adjust habitat rules, do not replace it silently.

title: Teach long division on pavement with chalk
mechanism_check: Confirm the real shortage: not enough desk space or the room is unusable — the pavement is a bigger board, not a punishment.
Check the surface: smooth concrete or asphalt holds chalk; gravel or wet ground does not.
Verify sun and sightline: chalk glare in direct sun is unreadable — work in the shade side of the building.
improvised_tools: Sidewalk chalk, thick sticks that do not snap under pressure
The pavement as a board ten times the classroom size
Students as human place-value markers standing on the digits
steps: Draw the division bracket huge — one problem per square yard, digits a foot tall.
Walk the algorithm aloud: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down — one student voices each step.
Station students on the digits: the '7' student stands on the 7 and announces their role.
Run three problems: you lead the first, the class calls the second, a student leads the third.
Photograph or copy the work back inside before rain, feet, or the bell erase it.
stop_conditions: Stop if weather or foot traffic makes the surface unsafe or unreadable — return inside rather than shouting over chaos.
Stop the human-place-value game if it becomes recess; the chalk work continues seated.
If a student is embarrassed standing on a digit, assign them the voice role instead — participation must stay voluntary.

title: Improvise anchor charts that students actually reference
mechanism_check: Check what the chart is for: a reference students consult during work, not wall decoration. If nobody looks at it mid-task, it failed.
Audit your wall space: charts must hang where students face during independent work, not behind the teacher's desk.
Confirm the chart's lifespan: a chart for one unit gets built cheap; a year-long reference earns the good paper.
improvised_tools: Butcher paper, newsprint, or taped-together copy paper as the chart body
Fat markers — thin pen lines are invisible from desks
Painter's tape for damage-free hanging and easy repositioning
steps: Title the chart with the exact question it answers: 'How do I start a paragraph?' not 'Writing.'
Build it WITH the class during the lesson — co-created charts get consulted; teacher-made charts get ignored.
Limit it to five or fewer elements: one visual, one rule, one example. More than that is wallpaper.
Hang it in the work sightline and physically point to it the first three times students need it — teach the reference habit.
Retire dead charts: take down what the class has internalized so the wall stays a tool, not a museum.
stop_conditions: Stop adding to a chart that already has five elements — start a second chart instead.
If the class never references it after two days, take it down and rebuild it smaller with them; do not let it fade into wallpaper.
Stop handwriting charts for a student who cannot read them from their seat — move their seat or rebuild bigger, same day.

title: Run a vocabulary lesson with nothing but voices and the board
mechanism_check: Identify which words actually need teaching: the five that unlock the text, not the twenty on the list. Teaching all of them teaches none.
Check pronunciation traps: if you cannot say it cleanly, the class will learn your version wrong — practice the hard words alone first.
Confirm the room can hear you: vocabulary taught in mumble is vocabulary misspelled on the test.
improvised_tools: The board: word, part of speech, one student-friendly definition, one example sentence
Choral repetition and call-and-response as the rehearsal engine
Student-generated gestures or sketches for the hardest two words
steps: Write each target word with its definition and one example sentence — never a word without a sentence.
Say it, class repeats it twice; clap the syllables so the shape of the word lands.
Cold-call individuals to use the word in a new sentence; fix usage on the spot, kindly and fast.
Run a 60-second partner quiz: one partner defines, the other guesses the word, then swap.
Exit ticket: three words used correctly in three original sentences.
stop_conditions: Stop if you catch yourself defining with harder words than the target word — redefine simpler or the lesson inverts.
Stop drilling a word the class clearly owns; move on to the next one rather than grinding confidence into boredom.
If a student's invented sentence reveals a wrong meaning, correct it publicly and immediately — wrong usage left standing becomes the class memory.

title: Improvise a math fluency game from a deck of cards
mechanism_check: Identify the fluency gap precisely: which facts are slow (7x8, 12-5)? The game must drill THAT set, not random arithmetic.
Check deck math: a standard deck minus face cards gives 1-10, perfect for facts practice; jokers become wild challenge cards.
Verify the room's tolerance for competition: some classes sharpen on it, others fracture — pick team mode for fragile classes.
improvised_tools: A standard deck of cards (face cards removed or repurposed as tens)
A scoreboard on the board — team names, tally marks, nothing fancy
A timer: 90-second rounds keep the energy from curdling into chaos
steps: Set the target fact family aloud: 'Tonight we own the sevens.'
Flip two cards; first team to call the product (or sum) takes the cards.
Wrong answers cost the turn — speed without accuracy loses, which teaches the real skill.
Rotate callers every round so the loudest student cannot carry the team.
End with the two slowest facts identified and drilled once more, slowly, as a class.
stop_conditions: Stop the game the moment taunting starts — competition that wounds is not a teaching tool; switch to team-vs-clock mode.
If one student dominates every round, change the rule (only non-callers may answer) rather than benching them.
Stop at the planned time even if it is close — a game that overstays becomes the lesson and the fluency goal evaporates.

title: Teach rhythm with desks, hands, and voice
mechanism_check: Confirm the concept: steady pulse first, patterns second. Students who cannot hold a pulse cannot play a rhythm.
Check the room's acoustic tolerance: desk-drumming travels through walls — warn the neighbor classroom or keep it to claps.
Verify physical limits: no drumming that hurts hands; palms on thighs, never knuckles on desks.
improvised_tools: Desk surfaces as drums (flat palms only)
Body percussion: claps, thigh slaps, snaps, stomps — four distinct timbres, zero equipment
Chanted syllables (ta, ti-ti) as the notation system before any written notes
steps: Establish the pulse: whole class claps quarter notes together for 30 seconds until it locks.
Layer one body-percussion ostinato: half the class keeps the pulse, half plays the pattern.
Notate it with syllables on the board so the pattern survives beyond the period.
Rotate parts so every student plays every layer at least once.
Close with a 16-beat performance: pulse group plus pattern group, one clean run.
stop_conditions: Stop if hands or desks are being hit hard enough to hurt — drop to claps and voice only.
If the pulse falls apart, strip back to pulse-only and rebuild; never layer onto a broken foundation.
Stop the performance push if the class is frustrated — play the pattern slowly together until it feels good, then try again.

title: Improvise art supplies from recycled materials
mechanism_check: Inventory what the room actually produces: paper scraps, cardboard, magazines, fabric offcuts, bottle caps — build the palette from the waste stream.
Check for hazards: no sharp metal, no glass shards, nothing with chemical residue; wash anything food-soiled first.
Confirm the project goal before gathering: collage needs flat colorful stock, sculpture needs rigid stock — gather to the project, not at random.
improvised_tools: Magazines, junk mail, and packaging as color and texture stock
Cardboard, egg cartons, and bottle caps as sculpture armatures
Flour-and-water paste as glue when the glue sticks run out
steps: Sort the gathered material by color and texture before starting — a sorted pile is a palette, an unsorted pile is trash.
Demo the single joining technique the project needs (paste layering, tab-and-slot, wrapping) before anyone builds.
Set the constraint that makes it art: one color family, one material, or one theme — limits force invention.
Circulate with the one question that helps: 'What is it missing?' not 'What is it?'
Display everything; the display wall is the second half of the lesson.
stop_conditions: Stop gathering the moment the pile exceeds what the project can use — excess material becomes a cleanup disaster, not a resource.
Reject any material that is dirty, sharp, or chemically suspect; no project is worth a cut or a rash.
If paste or paint starts going on walls and clothes instead of projects, pause and re-demo the technique — the medium is not the misbehavior.

title: Hold a reading lesson with a single shared book
mechanism_check: Check the text length against the period: a single-book lesson needs a passage short enough to read twice aloud.
Verify sightlines: one book means the teacher reads and the class listens — this is an oral-comprehension lesson, not silent reading.
Identify the two or three hard passages in advance; you will stop and unpack exactly those, nowhere else.
improvised_tools: The one book, read aloud with deliberate pacing
Prediction pauses: stop before the turn and take three predictions
The board for tracking: characters, questions, one-sentence summaries per section
steps: Set the listening job before opening the book: 'Listen for why the character lies — we will argue about it.'
Read aloud with pace changes: slow for the hard passages, brisk for the bridges.
Pause at your pre-marked spots: one question, three hands, move on — do not discuss every paragraph.
After reading, students write the one-sentence summary; read three aloud and let the class pick the truest.
Assign the re-read: tonight they re-read the same passage silently and find one detail they missed.
stop_conditions: Stop reading aloud if attention collapses — switch to student readers in short turns rather than pushing through.
Stop pausing if every pause kills momentum; some classes need the story's pull more than the analysis — bank the questions for after.
If the text is above the class's reach even read aloud, stop and switch to a shorter passage; finishing a hard book badly teaches that reading is suffering.

title: Run a classroom debate with no prep materials
mechanism_check: Confirm the topic is genuinely arguable from the students' own knowledge — no research means no obscure topics; use the lived and the studied.
Check the class's conflict temperature: a debate needs enough heat to argue and enough respect to stop; if the class cannot disagree kindly yet, run a structured discussion instead.
Verify you have a timer and a visible score or speaking-order system — unstructured debate becomes loudest-voice-wins.
improvised_tools: The board split into claim / evidence / rebuttal columns
A speaking order (alternating sides, 60 seconds each) enforced by the timer
Student judges: a panel of three who score on evidence, not volume
steps: State the motion in one sentence and give 3 minutes of silent side-picking and argument listing.
Opening statements: one speaker per side, 60 seconds, no interruptions.
Rebuttal rounds: alternating speakers must answer the other side's last point before making their own.
Judges deliberate aloud for 2 minutes, scoring evidence quality, then declare a winner.
Close by naming the strongest argument from the LOSING side — the lesson is that good arguments exist everywhere.
stop_conditions: Stop the debate the moment it turns personal — one warning, then the round ends and the class debriefs what crossed the line.
If one side has no arguments after the prep time, pause and give both sides 2 more minutes; a slaughter teaches nothing.
Stop adding rounds when the arguments start repeating — call the judges in while the energy is still high.

title: Improvise a measurement lab with cups, string, and a kitchen timer
mechanism_check: Identify the measurement concept: unit, iteration, or estimation. The lab must make one of them physical.
Check consistency of your improvised units: a 'cup' varies by cup — calibrate once against a single reference cup and mark it.
Verify the timer situation: one kitchen timer plus student counting beats five unsynced phone timers.
improvised_tools: A single marked reference cup as the unit standard
String cut to reference lengths (the 'meter' of the day)
A kitchen timer plus a student caller counting seconds aloud
steps: Calibrate publicly: fill the reference cup, pour it into three other cups, mark which ones match — the class now owns the unit.
Pose the measurement question: 'How many cups fill the bucket? How many strings long is the room?'
Teams measure twice and compare; disagreement is the lesson, not a failure.
Record results in a shared table on the board; compute the class average.
Name the mechanism: standard units exist because improvised units disagree — that is why the meter was invented.
stop_conditions: Stop if spilled water makes the floor unsafe — mop first, measure second; the lab resumes dry.
If teams' numbers disagree wildly, do not average garbage — recalibrate the unit and re-measure.
Stop adding new measurements once the concept lands; three clean data points beat ten sloppy ones.

title: Teach geography with a hand-drawn floor map
mechanism_check: Confirm the spatial concept: relative position, scale, or routes. The floor map must serve one of them.
Check the floor space: you need a clear area big enough for students to stand on countries without tripping.
Verify the map's proportions before class: a wildly wrong shape teaches a wrong mental image that sticks for years.
improvised_tools: Masking tape or chalk for borders on the floor
Paper labels for place names, taped down where they belong
Students themselves as travelers, trade goods, or weather systems moving across the map
steps: Draw the region's outline large on the floor; label the anchor places students already know.
Walk the first route yourself, narrating: 'From here to here crosses this — what changes?'
Assign students as travelers with a mission: reach the destination using only the labeled places.
Introduce one disruption: a blocked pass, a closed port — the class must re-route.
Close by transferring the floor map to paper: each student sketches it from memory and labels five places.
stop_conditions: Stop if the map's shapes are wrong — erase and redraw rather than teaching a distorted world.
If students start treating the floor as a playground, return to desks and finish the transfer-to-paper step early.
Stop adding places once the map is crowded; five well-known places beat twenty forgotten ones.

title: Run a reading block with no library through a book exchange
mechanism_check: Count actual books in the room: a reading block needs roughly one book per two students minimum, or it is a waiting block.
Check reading-level spread: a single stack of one-level books strands both the strugglers and the sprinters.
Verify the exchange logistics: who tracks the books, where do they live, what happens to a lost one — decide before opening.
improvised_tools: Every book in the room pooled into one class shelf, leveled roughly by the teacher
A checkout log: name, title, date — paper notebook, one line per book
A 'book talk' minute: each returning student pitches the book in 30 seconds
steps: Pool all books into one visible shelf; let students browse for 5 minutes before choosing.
Launch the exchange with the one rule that matters: return it in the condition you got it, or you replace the log entry with an apology and a repair job.
Run 20 minutes of silent reading — you read too, visibly; a reading teacher who grades papers during reading time kills the culture.
Close with two book talks: students pitch, class decides who wants it next — the waitlist is the engine.
Weekly, cull the unreadable and celebrate the most-passed-around book.
stop_conditions: Stop the block if there are truly too few books — switch to the single-shared-book lesson (educational-013) rather than faking a library.
If books start disappearing, pause the exchange, audit the log publicly, and restart with a checkout buddy system.
Stop forcing a book on a student who hates it after 20 pages — the rule is 'abandon and choose again,' not 'finish and resent.'

title: Improvise an outdoor classroom in five minutes
mechanism_check: Check the weather and ground honestly: damp grass plus paper equals a ruined lesson; heat plus sun equals wilted attention.
Scan for the seating geometry: a circle or arc where everyone sees you — a scattered crowd is a recess, not a class.
Confirm the learning goal fits outdoors: observation, discussion, and movement thrive; fine print and tests do not.
improvised_tools: A boundary: cones, a rope, or 'the bench line' — the class needs to know where class is
Clipboards or hard books as writing surfaces on laps
Your voice projected at 120%: outdoors eats volume, so teach in shorter bursts
steps: Set the boundary first, before any content: 'Class is inside this line.'
Arrange the arc, backs to the distraction (parking lot, playground), faces to you.
Teach in 5-minute bursts with a movement or pair-share between each — outdoor attention decays fast.
Use the environment as the material: count, measure, observe, or discuss what is actually around you.
Close back inside: the last 5 minutes happen at desks where the notes get written down properly.
stop_conditions: Stop and go inside if weather turns, insects swarm, or another class's noise makes hearing impossible.
If the boundary dissolves twice, the outdoor lesson is over — finish seated inside rather than herding.
Never run an assessment outdoors; wind, sun, and laps corrupt the results.

title: Design a lesson backward from the objective
mechanism_check: Check whether you actually have an objective or just a topic: 'fractions' is a topic; 'students will add fractions with unlike denominators' is an objective. Topics cannot be designed backward from.
Verify the objective is assessable in the period: if you cannot picture the proof the student got it, the objective is too big.
Confirm the students' starting point honestly: the lesson bridges from where they ARE, not where the pacing guide wishes they were.
improvised_tools: One sentence objective, written first and never edited mid-lesson
The exit ticket designed second — the assessment before the activities
A three-column plan: objective, proof (assessment), path (activities that earn the proof)
steps: Write the objective as a student-can-do sentence.
Design the exit ticket next: the exact task that proves the objective was met.
Plan only the activities that directly earn that proof; cut everything else.
Sequence: hook (2 min), model (7 min), guided practice, independent proof (the exit ticket).
After teaching, sort the exit tickets into got-it / close / lost and let the sort design tomorrow's lesson.
stop_conditions: Stop planning activities before the objective and assessment exist — activity-first planning is how lessons drift.
If the exit ticket proves the objective was wrong (too easy, everyone aces it), fix the objective tomorrow; do not punish success.
Stop adding 'enrichment' the class has not earned: if half the class is lost, the next lesson is reteach, not extension.

title: Build a rubric that grades fairly
mechanism_check: Check what the assignment actually asked students to do: the rubric must measure the objective, not neatness, length, or effort vibes.
Verify you can picture the difference between each level: if 'good' and 'great' blur in your head, they will blur in grading.
Confirm the rubric fits the assignment's weight: a 4-criterion rubric on a 10-point quiz is grading theater.
improvised_tools: Three to four criteria, each tied to one observable skill
Student work samples (anonymized) to anchor each level before grading
The rubric handed out WITH the assignment, never revealed at grading time
steps: List the 3-4 skills the assignment was built to teach — these become the criteria.
Write the top level first: what does excellent actually look like, concretely?
Write the bottom level: what does missing look like? Fill the middle last.
Test-grade three samples against it; if two samples land ambiguously, rewrite the blurry criterion.
Give the rubric to students with the assignment and let them self-score before submitting.
stop_conditions: Stop adding criteria beyond four — each extra criterion doubles grading time and halves student attention to any of them.
If you find yourself overriding the rubric while grading ('I know what I meant'), the rubric is wrong; fix the words, not the scores.
Never grade on criteria students never saw; if it mattered, it belonged on the rubric they received.

title: Ask questions that make thinking visible
mechanism_check: Audit your last lesson's questions honestly: if 90% had one-word answers, you were quizzing recall, not teaching thinking.
Check wait time: the average teacher waits under 1 second; thinking needs 3-5. Your questions are only as good as your silence.
Verify the room's answer safety: if wrong answers get laughed at, only the brave will think aloud.
improvised_tools: Planned hinge questions: 2-3 per lesson, written in the plan, that the lesson pivots on
Mandatory 3-second wait time after every real question — count it silently
No-hands-up cold calling balanced with think-pair-share so everyone rehearses before exposure
steps: Ask the question to the whole class first, then name the respondent — order matters; name-first lets everyone else stop thinking.
Wait a full 3 seconds of real silence; do not rescue them from the thinking.
Probe the answer, right or wrong: 'What makes you say that?' — the reasoning is the lesson, not the answer.
Bounce it: 'Who can build on that?' — thinking becomes a group construction.
Close the exchange by restating the refined idea so the class hears the finished thought.
stop_conditions: Stop calling only on raised hands — you are sampling the confident, not teaching the room.
If you answer your own question twice in a row, stop and write the next question down instead of improvising it; improvised questions collapse to recall.
Stop probing when a student is visibly shutting down; take their partial answer, thank them, and bounce to a peer.

title: Give feedback students will act on
mechanism_check: Check whether your feedback is actionable: 'good job' and 'be clearer' are verdicts, not instructions. If the student cannot picture the next step, it is not feedback.
Verify timing: feedback on work from three weeks ago is archaeology; the fresher the work, the more the feedback lands.
Confirm the volume: ten comments on one paper means none of them get read. The brain processes two corrections at a time.
improvised_tools: Two comments maximum per piece: one strength to keep, one specific fix to make
The fix stated as a do-this: 'Start each paragraph with your claim' not 'unclear structure'
A 5-minute revision window in class where the feedback gets used immediately
steps: Name exactly what worked and why: 'Your second example proves the claim — keep leading with evidence.'
Give the single highest-leverage fix as an instruction, with an example of the fixed version.
Build in class time to apply it now — feedback without revision time is a monologue.
Collect the revision and check only whether the fix was applied; grade the growth, not just the product.
Track which fixes recur across the class; the recurring one becomes tomorrow's mini-lesson.
stop_conditions: Stop writing more than two comments per paper — you are editing, not teaching, and the student will read none of it.
If the same feedback repeats on the same student three times with no change, stop writing it and conference face-to-face; the written channel has failed.
Never give feedback only as a grade; a number without words teaches nothing except rank.

title: Install a classroom routine that runs itself
mechanism_check: Identify the friction point: the 5 minutes lost every period to the same chaos (entry, materials, transitions). One routine fixes one friction; do not install five at once.
Check what the students currently do by default: the routine must replace an existing habit, and habits need a cue, not just a rule.
Verify you can enforce it consistently for two weeks: a routine you drop on day four teaches that routines are optional.
improvised_tools: A visible cue: the bell-work prompt already on the board when they enter
Assigned roles that rotate weekly: materials manager, timekeeper, greeter
A 3-step posted procedure for the single most chaotic transition
steps: Pick the ONE transition that bleeds the most time; ignore the rest for now.
Teach the routine explicitly like content: model it, rehearse it, correct it — three days minimum.
Post the steps where the transition happens, not on a distant wall.
Narrate compliance early: 'Materials team is already moving — thank you.' Praise the routine, not individuals.
After two smooth weeks, hand the cue to a student role and install the next routine.
stop_conditions: Stop installing a second routine before the first runs without you — stacked routines collapse together.
If the routine needs your constant narration after two weeks, it is too complicated; simplify the steps, do not shout louder.
Stop and reteach the moment the routine degrades; a routine you let slide is a routine you uninstalled.

title: Differentiate on the fly without extra prep
mechanism_check: Check what 'different' the moment actually needs: pace (slower/faster), entry point (concrete/abstract), or output mode (write/speak/draw). Diagnose before differentiating.
Verify you know the spread: which three students are lost, which three are done early — differentiation without names is just vibes.
Confirm the core task is solid first: differentiating a broken task multiplies the breakage.
improvised_tools: Tiered questioning: same discussion, deeper follow-ups for the ready, concrete reframes for the lost
Choice of output: answer in words, a sketch, or an explanation to a partner — same thinking, three doors
The early-finisher extension kept in your head: 'Now prove it a second way' or 'Teach it to your neighbor'
steps: Launch the whole class on the same core task — no separate worksheets, no visible tracks.
Circulate in the first 3 minutes and tag your lost-three and done-three by name.
Drop scaffolds verbally to the lost: a worked first step, a simpler number, a partner.
Feed extensions to the done: a second method, a 'what if' twist, a teaching assignment.
Close with the whole class on the same exit ticket — one standard, multiple paths to it.
stop_conditions: Stop if your 'differentiation' becomes a permanent lower track — scaffolds must fade as students climb, or you have built a ceiling.
If you cannot name who needs what by minute three, stop differentiating and reteach the core; you are guessing.
Never announce the tiers ('my low group'); the class must experience one lesson with invisible supports.

title: Read student errors to find the misconception
mechanism_check: Sort the errors before reacting: are many students making the SAME wrong move, or is every error different? Same error means a class misconception; scattered errors mean individual gaps.
Check whether the error is procedural (wrong steps) or conceptual (wrong idea): procedural errors need practice, conceptual errors need reteaching — the fixes are opposites.
Verify against the last lesson: did you actually teach the thing they are getting wrong, or did you assume it was prior knowledge?
improvised_tools: A quick error sort: three piles — same-wrong-answer, same-wrong-method, scattered
Two or three student interviews: 'Walk me through how you got this' — the transcript reveals the logic
The board as a diagnostic space: work the error publicly without naming the student
steps: Collect the work and sort errors into patterns before the next class — 10 minutes of sorting beats an hour of blind reteaching.
Name the misconception in one sentence: 'They are adding denominators because they treat fractions as two separate whole numbers.'
Design tomorrow's opener to break exactly that idea: one counterexample that makes the misconception impossible.
Teach the confrontation directly: show the error, show why it breaks, show the repair.
Re-assess with one parallel problem; if the pattern persists, the misconception is deeper than one lesson.
stop_conditions: Stop reteaching the whole unit when the error is one misconception — surgical reteach, not carpet-bombing.
If the interview reveals the student never learned the prerequisite at all, stop and backfill the prerequisite; no shortcut exists.
Stop marking errors wrong without diagnosing at least the pattern; unexamined errors repeat on the test.

title: Write a parent message that builds an ally
mechanism_check: Check the relationship balance: if every prior contact was a complaint, this message lands as another complaint no matter how you phrase it. Lead with something true and positive.
Verify your facts: names, dates, what actually happened — one wrong detail destroys your credibility for the year.
Confirm the ask: what do you need from the parent? A message without a clear, small ask is just a notification.
improvised_tools: The 2:1 structure: two specific positives, one concern, one concrete ask
Specific observations, never labels: 'left seat three times during math' not 'disruptive'
A reply window: 'I am available to talk Tuesday after 3' — an open door, not an open wound
steps: Open with something specific and true the student did well — not flattery, evidence.
State the concern as observed behavior with date, no diagnosis, no labels.
Make one small, concrete ask: 'Please ask him about the math homework tonight' — parents act on small asks.
Offer the conversation, not the verdict: 'I would love to hear your read on this.'
Log the message and any reply in one place; follow up in one week whether or not they responded.
stop_conditions: Stop writing if you are angry — draft it, wait an hour, cut every sentence you would not say face-to-face.
Never put a diagnosis, a comparison to siblings, or another family's business in writing; those are conversation-only, if ever.
If the parent becomes hostile, stop the thread and move to a mediated conversation with admin present; do not win the email war.

title: Level up your credential portfolio deliberately
mechanism_check: Audit where you actually stand: current certification, endorsements, years, and what your district pays a premium for. Credentials without a pay or role payoff are hobbies.
Check the real requirements, not the rumor: your state's licensing board site, your district's salary schedule — get the documents.
Verify the time cost honestly: a National Board portfolio is 200+ hours; a micro-credential is 15. Match the investment to the payoff.
improvised_tools: Your district's salary schedule as the ROI map
A one-page portfolio log: credential, cost, hours, payoff, deadline
Colleagues who already hold the credential — their hindsight is worth more than any brochure
steps: List every credential that changes your pay, your assignment options, or your security; rank by payoff per hour.
Pick ONE target per year — stacked credential pursuits all fail together.
Map the requirements backward from the deadline into weekly blocks on your calendar.
Document as you go: every artifact, every hour, filed the week it happens — portfolios assembled from memory lose.
When earned, file the paperwork the same week and confirm the salary or assignment change in writing.
stop_conditions: Stop pursuing a credential whose payoff you cannot name in one sentence — 'growth' is not a payoff, it is a hope.
If the pursuit is degrading your classroom performance, pause it; no credential outranks the students in front of you.
Stop collecting free certificates that change nothing; one earned board certification beats ten webinar badges.

title: Mentor a first-year teacher so they stay
mechanism_check: Diagnose which crisis they are actually in: classroom management, planning overload, parent conflict, or isolation. New teachers report 'everything' — your job is to find the one fire.
Check your own bandwidth honestly: a mentor who flakes does more damage than no mentor; commit to the cadence you can keep.
Verify the power dynamic: you are not their evaluator. Say it explicitly, or they will hide the real problems.
improvised_tools: A fixed weekly 30-minute slot — same time, same place, non-negotiable
Classroom visits in both directions: you watch them, they watch you
A shared 'wins and wrecks' log: one line each per week, no judgment
steps: First meeting: name the non-evaluator rule and ask for their one biggest fire this week.
Solve the fire first — give them the concrete thing (a routine, a script, a plan) before any philosophy.
Observe their class within two weeks; give exactly two notes: one keep, one fix.
Invite them to observe your hardest class, not your best — they need to see struggle handled, not perfection.
Monthly, ask the retention question directly: 'What would make you quit? What would make you stay?'
stop_conditions: Stop giving advice the week you stop listening — a mentor who lectures is just a second evaluator.
If their struggle is a building-level problem (abusive admin, impossible assignment), stop coaching around it and escalate with them; mentoring cannot fix systems.
End the formal mentorship if it becomes dependency — the goal is a colleague, not a client.

title: Run a weekly self-observation to fix one habit
mechanism_check: Pick ONE habit to observe — talk time, wait time, circulation pattern, question quality. Observing everything observes nothing.
Check your data source honestly: memory lies. You need a tally, a timer, or a recording — something that counts.
Verify the habit is actually fixable by you this month, not a building condition (class size, schedule) you cannot change.
improvised_tools: A phone voice memo recording one lesson per week (students' voices only matter in aggregate — check your school's recording policy first)
A simple tally sheet: one mark per teacher-talk minute, per question type, per student contacted
A colleague's 10-minute drop-in as the outside eye once a month
steps: Choose the one habit and define its measure: 'I will count my talk-minutes per 45-minute lesson.'
Collect one lesson of data — tally, timer, or recording.
Review for 15 minutes that week: where did the habit help, where did it cost?
Set one micro-adjustment for next week: 'I will pause 3 seconds after questions in period 2.'
Re-measure in two weeks; keep what moved the number, drop what did not.
stop_conditions: Stop if you are collecting data you never review — unreviewed tallies are guilt paperwork; either review weekly or stop collecting.
If the recording policy forbids it, stop recording and use the tally method; never violate student privacy for self-improvement.
Stop chasing more than one habit per month; habit change is slow and stacked goals all fail.

title: Track one class metric without a spreadsheet app
mechanism_check: Choose ONE metric that predicts what you care about: exit-ticket mastery rate, on-task percentage, homework return rate. One metric, tracked daily, beats a dashboard you never open.
Check the collection cost: if it takes more than 2 minutes per class, you will abandon it by Friday.
Verify the metric is honest: 'participation vibes' is not a metric; counted raised hands or completed tickets are.
improvised_tools: A paper grid taped inside your plan book: rows are days, columns are class periods
Tally marks or a 1-5 rating per period, recorded in the last 60 seconds of class
A weekly 5-minute review: circle the best and worst day, ask why
steps: Define the metric in one countable sentence: 'Exit tickets scoring 3 or higher, as a fraction of the class.'
Build the grid: 5 rows (days) by N columns (periods), one cell per class per day.
Record it in the final minute of class, every class, no exceptions — the streak is the system.
Friday, spend 5 minutes: which day was best, which worst, what was different?
After three weeks, change ONE thing and watch the metric for two more weeks; that is your experiment.
stop_conditions: Stop tracking a metric you never act on — data without decisions is decoration.
If recording takes more than 2 minutes, simplify the metric; a coarse metric you keep beats a fine one you drop.
Stop adding a second metric before the first has driven one real change.

title: Hold a repair conversation after a behavior blow-up
mechanism_check: Check your own state first: if you are still angry, the conversation will be a second punishment. Cool down fully — the repair happens tomorrow, not today.
Verify the facts: what happened, who saw it, what the consequence already was. Repair is separate from consequence; do not re-litigate the punishment.
Confirm the student's state: a hungry, humiliated, or exhausted student cannot repair anything yet; meet the need first.
improvised_tools: A private 5-minute window — hallway, after class, never in front of peers
The three-question script: what happened, who was affected, what will you do differently
A clean-slate statement you mean: 'Tomorrow we start fresh.'
steps: Wait until you are genuinely calm — hours or a day, not minutes.
Pull the student aside privately; state the purpose in one line: 'I want us to fix this, not replay it.'
Ask the three questions and actually listen; do not correct their version mid-answer.
Name the impact on the class plainly, without shaming: 'When that happened, the lesson stopped for everyone.'
Agree on the one different choice for next time, shake on the clean slate, and keep it — treat them normally the next day.
stop_conditions: Stop the conversation if either of you is escalating; reschedule rather than forcing a repair that becomes round two.
If the behavior involves harm, threats, or illegality, stop the repair script and follow the school's safety protocol — repair never replaces reporting.
Stop bringing up the incident after the repair is done; a clean slate you keep mentioning is not clean.

title: Plan a week of lessons in one sitting
mechanism_check: Check the week's real constraints first: assemblies, testing, short days, your energy dips. Plan around the week you have, not the ideal week.
Verify the through-line: five disconnected lessons are five times the prep; one weekly arc with daily variations is one prep stretched five ways.
Confirm your materials reality: what is already made, copied, or improvised from last year — never plan a week that requires five nights of building.
improvised_tools: A one-page weekly grid: day, objective, proof (exit ticket), materials needed
Last year's plans as the starting draft — plagiarize yourself freely
A 'bank' of 10-minute activities (educational-001 through 014) for gaps and short days
steps: Write Monday's objective, then let each day's objective build on the last — the arc, not five islands.
Design each day's exit ticket before its activities (backward design, every day).
Batch the materials: one copy run, one supply gather, for the whole week.
Mark the two heaviest days and keep the other three light — you cannot sprint five days.
Leave Friday's last 15 minutes unplanned: that is the buffer the week will need.
stop_conditions: Stop planning when the sitting hits 90 minutes — diminishing returns after that; the rest gets planned Sunday night.
If a day requires materials you do not have and cannot improvise, redesign the day rather than hoping supplies appear.
Stop re-planning mid-week unless the exit tickets demand it; trust the arc and adjust next week.

title: Co-teach a period with station rotation
mechanism_check: Check the real coordination challenge: two adults, one room, one period — without assigned roles you get one teacher and one expensive aide.
Verify parity before the period: both teachers must know the objective and their station; a briefing in the hallway is not planning.
Confirm the student grouping: stations need groups formed before the bell, or the first 10 minutes evaporate.
improvised_tools: Three stations, three roles: direct-teach, guided practice, independent application — one teacher per adult-led station
A visible timer both teachers honor; the rotation is sacred
A one-line shared plan: objective, station jobs, who handles behavior
steps: Split the class into three pre-made groups before the period starts.
Teacher A runs the direct-teach station (the new content), Teacher B runs guided practice, station three is independent.
Rotate every 12-15 minutes on the timer; no station runs long because 'they were just getting it.'
Both teachers circulate during the independent station's rotation to check the exit work.
Debrief for 5 minutes after: what did each station reveal about mastery? Adjust tomorrow together.
stop_conditions: Stop the model if one teacher consistently becomes the aide — reassign roles explicitly next period, or co-teaching is just expensive solo teaching.
If behavior collapses during rotations, stop and run the period as parallel teaching (split the class in halves) until routines are solid.
Stop adding stations beyond three; more stations means thinner teaching at each.

title: Run a 20-minute grade-level team huddle
mechanism_check: Check the coordination challenge: teachers share students but not information — the huddle exists to move student knowledge, not to socialize.
Verify the time is actually protected: a huddle that gets bumped for everything teaches the team it does not matter.
Confirm everyone brings one thing: without input the huddle is a meeting about nothing.
improvised_tools: A standing agenda with three slots: wins (3 min), stuck students (10 min), logistics (5 min), decisions (2 min)
A shared student watchlist: names the team is jointly tracking, updated live
One decision log: what was decided, who owns it, by when — one page, kept by a rotating scribe
steps: Start on time even if someone is missing; punctuality is the team's first agreement.
Wins first, 3 minutes: one concrete student win per teacher — the huddle opens with evidence, not complaints.
Stuck students, 10 minutes: name the student, the pattern, the one team action. No student gets more than 3 minutes.
Logistics, 5 minutes: dates, coverage, materials — fast, factual, no discussion.
Close with decisions read back: who does what by when. The scribe sends the log the same day.
stop_conditions: Stop the huddle at 20 minutes even mid-topic; the unfinished item becomes next week's first item — overrun kills the habit.
If the huddle becomes a complaint session two weeks running, stop and reset the agenda; venting without decisions is not teamwork.
If a member never brings input and never takes actions, address it privately; a passenger eventually sinks the huddle.

title: Do a team lesson-study on one stubborn standard
mechanism_check: Check the coordination challenge: every teacher teaches the standard differently, so nobody knows which version works — the study compares versions honestly.
Verify the standard is genuinely stubborn: exit-ticket data shows low mastery across classrooms, not just one.
Confirm psychological safety: teachers must show their real lessons, including the flops, or the study compares performances, not practice.
improvised_tools: One shared standard and one shared assessment, agreed before anyone teaches
Observation notes focused on student thinking, not teacher performance
A debrief protocol: what did students do, what does it mean, what changes next
steps: The team picks the standard and writes the common assessment together — the yardstick comes first.
One teacher teaches the lesson while the others observe student work and thinking, not the teacher.
Debrief within 24 hours: sort student responses, name the misconceptions the lesson did and did not move.
A second teacher re-teaches the revised lesson to their class; the team observes again.
Publish the findings to the team in one page: what worked, the revised lesson plan, the data.
stop_conditions: Stop if observations become teacher evaluations — the moment anyone feels judged, the honesty ends and so does the study.
If the data shows no difference between versions, stop tweaking delivery and question the standard's sequencing; the problem may be upstream.
Stop after two cycles per standard; diminishing returns set in and the team needs its planning time back.

title: Cover a colleague's class without losing your prep
mechanism_check: Check the coordination challenge: coverage is a team debt system — today you pay, tomorrow you collect; without the ledger, resentment compounds.
Verify what the absent teacher actually left: a real plan, a vague note, or nothing. Your response scales to what exists.
Confirm your own non-negotiables: which 15 minutes of your prep are untouchable, and what can flex.
improvised_tools: A team coverage ledger: who covered whom, when — visible to all, settled monthly
The emergency lesson bank: five no-prep lessons (from this pack) any teacher can run cold
The absent teacher's seating chart and the two students who can brief you in 60 seconds
steps: Read the plan (or the lack of it) and pick the response tier: real plan means run it; vague note means run the emergency bank lesson; nothing means run your own bank lesson on their topic.
Ask the two briefing students for the class's current state in 60 seconds: where they are, who needs watching.
Run the lesson; keep it simpler than your own class would get — coverage is continuity, not excellence.
Leave a one-paragraph note: what got done, who struggled, what is left.
Log the coverage in the ledger the same day; the team settles the balance, not your memory.
stop_conditions: Stop covering if the same teacher's absences always land on you — take the ledger to the team lead; coverage is shared or it is exploitation.
If the class has no plan and no bank lesson fits, stop improvising content and run a structured study/review period; a calm room beats a chaotic lesson.
Never sacrifice the prep period you need to teach your own classes well tomorrow; protect the minimum or the debt spreads.

title: Run a team data review that ends in one action
mechanism_check: Check the coordination challenge: data reviews die two ways — no data (opinions meeting) or too much data (paralysis meeting). One shared dataset, pre-read.
Verify the data is comparable: same assessment, same scoring, or the comparison is fiction.
Confirm the decision authority: the team must be able to act on what it finds, or the review is theater.
improvised_tools: One page per teacher: mastery rate on the common assessment, plus the two most-missed items
A pre-read rule: the numbers are read before the meeting, the meeting is for decisions
The action template: we will ___ for ___ students, starting ___, measured by ___
steps: Open with the headline numbers, 5 minutes, no discussion — just the facts on the table.
Each teacher names their two most-missed items; the team circles the overlaps — the shared wound is the target.
Ask the mechanism question together: what misconception explains the overlap? (See educational-025.)
Write the ONE action in the template: specific, owned, dated, measured.
Set the re-measure date now — usually two weeks — and put it on the calendar before leaving the room.
stop_conditions: Stop the review if it becomes teacher-blame; the data describes student learning, not teacher worth — redirect once, end the meeting if it continues.
If the data is not comparable, stop comparing and spend the meeting building the common assessment instead.
Stop at one action; a review that produces five actions produces zero actions.

title: Split planning across a team without doubling work
mechanism_check: Check the coordination challenge: shared planning fails when everyone plans everything (duplication) or when one person plans everything (resentment). The split must be explicit.
Verify compatibility: shared lessons only work if the team agrees on the objective and assessment first; style can differ, standards cannot.
Confirm the handoff format: a lesson plan your colleague cannot read in 5 minutes is not shared, it is donated confusion.
improvised_tools: A unit map: which teacher owns which lesson, with dates — one page, visible to all
A common plan template: objective, assessment, materials, 5-minute read time maximum
A shared drive folder or binder with the unit's materials, filed by lesson
steps: Map the unit together: divide lessons by strength and interest, not just evenly — the best explainer takes the hardest concept.
Agree on the common assessments first; individual lessons can vary, the yardstick cannot.
Each teacher writes their owned lessons in the common template and files them by the agreed date.
Teach, then report back one line per lesson: what worked, what flopped — the notes become next year's plan.
Rotate ownership next unit so expertise spreads and no one becomes the permanent planner.
stop_conditions: Stop the split if one teacher's lessons consistently arrive late or unusable — address it directly; the team is not a charity for planning.
If shared lessons require heavy adaptation to be teachable, the template is wrong; fix the template, not each lesson.
Stop splitting if the team cannot agree on assessments; without a common yardstick, shared planning is just file-sharing.

title: Repair a team conflict before it reaches the principal
mechanism_check: Diagnose the conflict type: task conflict (what to do — healthy, solvable) versus relationship conflict (who is wrong — toxic, escalating). Most team fights are task conflicts wearing relationship masks.
Check the history: is this the first flare or the tenth? A pattern means the system needs fixing, not the people.
Verify you are a neutral party or at least a trusted one; a combatant cannot mediate their own fight.
improvised_tools: A private conversation, not a team meeting — conflicts get honest in pairs, performative in groups
The interests script: 'What do you need to happen?' asked of each side separately
A written agreement of the resolution, however small — memory rewrites verbal deals
steps: Talk to each person separately first: what happened, what do you need, what would resolve it.
Name the task conflict underneath: strip the personalities until the real disagreement shows.
Bring them together with the framed problem: 'You both want the unit to work; you disagree on the pacing.'
Negotiate the specific behavior change, not the attitude change: 'Plans filed by Thursday' not 'be more respectful.'
Write the agreement, both sign off, check in after two weeks — and keep it off the principal's desk if it holds.
stop_conditions: Stop mediating and escalate if the conflict involves harassment, discrimination, or sabotage — those are administrative matters, not team matters.
If one party refuses every private conversation, stop; you cannot mediate an empty chair — escalate with documentation.
Stop if you are one of the combatants and cannot be neutral; recuse yourself and ask the team lead to step in.

title: Combine subjects into one team project week
mechanism_check: Check the coordination challenge: interdisciplinary projects collapse when subjects just decorate each other (the 'math poster about history'); real combination means each subject's skill is required to finish.
Verify the schedule reality: you need aligned periods or a restructured week — get admin approval before promising students.
Confirm the assessment plan: who grades what, or the project becomes everyone's and no one's.
improvised_tools: One driving question that genuinely needs every subject: 'Design a working water filter and argue for its adoption' needs science, math, writing, and art
A shared rubric with one criterion per subject, built together (see educational-020)
A public exhibition at the end — an audience makes the work real
steps: The team agrees on the driving question and the non-negotiable skill each subject contributes.
Build the shared rubric together; each teacher owns their subject's criterion.
Launch together: all teachers present the question in one joint session so students feel the scale.
Run the week with daily 10-minute teacher huddles to adjust pacing and catch struggling groups.
Exhibit publicly: parents, other classes, admin — then debrief the team on what to keep and cut.
stop_conditions: Stop if one subject becomes decoration — either give it a real required skill or cut it from the project honestly.
If the schedule cannot be aligned, stop and run it as a two-subject project; a forced four-subject week with no shared time is chaos.
Stop adding scope mid-week; the project that grows daily never finishes.

title: Onboard a new teacher onto the team in 30 days
mechanism_check: Check the coordination challenge: new teachers drown in unwritten rules — the onboarding must surface the invisible (who to ask, where things live, how decisions get made).
Verify the buddy assignment: one named buddy, not 'the team' — diffuse responsibility means no responsibility.
Confirm the information diet: everything on day one means nothing retained; sequence it across the month.
improvised_tools: A 30-day checklist: week 1 survival, week 2 routines, week 3 students, week 4 independence
The buddy: one teacher, weekly 20-minute check-ins, first four weeks
The team's living documents: unit map, coverage ledger, huddle norms — handed over, not hidden
steps: Day one: the tour that matters — copier, supply closet, who to call for what, the bathroom code. Survival first.
Week one: buddy co-plans the first week; the new teacher teaches with training wheels, not alone.
Week two: hand over the routines (educational-023) and the team's shared materials; observe one of their classes kindly.
Week three: introduce the watchlist students with context, not just names — the team's hard-won knowledge transfers.
Day thirty: a retro — what helped, what was missing — and the buddy steps back to on-call.
stop_conditions: Stop the buddy system from becoming permanent scaffolding; by day thirty the teacher should be planning solo with check-ins, not co-planning.
If the new teacher is struggling beyond normal ramp-up, stop onboarding-as-usual and pair it with mentoring (educational-028) or admin support.
Stop adding to the checklist once it works; a 30-day list that grows to 60 days is a different program.

title: Build a team emergency playbook for bad days
mechanism_check: Check the coordination challenge: bad days (absences, crises, lockdowns, tech failures) hit teams that never rehearsed — the playbook turns panic into procedure.
Verify the real scenarios: list the last year's actual bad days, not hypothetical disasters; the playbook covers what happened, not what might.
Confirm everyone knows where the playbook lives: a playbook nobody can find in the moment is a binder, not a tool.
improvised_tools: One page per scenario: trigger, first three actions, who decides, who communicates
A phone tree or group chat with the explicit rule: emergencies only, no chatter
The emergency lesson bank (from educational-036) attached as the teaching fallback
steps: The team lists its last year of bad days; pick the five most likely to recur.
For each, write the one-page play: trigger, first three actions, decision-maker, communicator.
Assign every role a backup — the playbook must survive the absence of any one person.
Rehearse once: walk through one scenario in a huddle, timed, and fix what is unclear.
Review yearly or after every real use; a playbook that never gets updated rots.
stop_conditions: Stop writing scenarios beyond the real five; a 40-page playbook never gets read in an emergency.
If a scenario requires admin or district action, stop at the handoff line — the playbook says who calls, not how to do their job.
Stop and rewrite any page that takes more than 60 seconds to understand; in the moment, complexity is the enemy.
